summary: Updates the Kerberos public-key initial authentication standard in RFC 4556 so it is no longer tied to specific cryptographic algorithms. The key derivation function becomes negotiable, and the digest algorithms for signing and for client certificates become discoverable. This allows newer algorithms to be rolled out gradually if old ones are found weak.

eli5.summary: Imagine a game that only works with one kind of lock. This change lets players agree on which lock to use, so a better lock can be swapped in if the old one breaks.

questions: how to change kerberos crypto algorithms
how does pkinit negotiate the kdf
subtitle: Lets Kerberos public-key logins negotiate their key derivation function and discover which hash algorithms a server accepts.

tldr.problem: PKINIT, the public-key way to log in to Kerberos, had parts hardwired to SHA-1 or left to local policy with no way to negotiate or discover algorithms, which became a concern after hash-function attacks were reported.
tldr.mechanism: The client lists the key derivation functions it supports, the KDC picks one, and new typed data in two error messages lets the KDC tell the client which digest algorithms it accepts.
tldr.outcome: Newer hash algorithms can be deployed step by step, and implementations MUST support id-pkinit-kdf-ah-sha256. The paChecksum stays fixed at SHA-1.

today: RFC 8636 is a Proposed Standard from July 2019 that updates RFC 4556. It has not been obsoleted or updated itself, so it is the current specification of PKINIT algorithm agility.

sections.title: Why PKINIT Needed Algorithm Agility
sections.content:
RFC 4556 defines PKINIT, which lets a Kerberos client use public key cryptography for its initial authentication. RFC 8636 updates it, because several PKINIT structures were either tied to SHA-1 or based on local policy with no negotiation or discovery:

  • The checksum algorithm in the authentication request is hardwired to SHA-1.
  • The acceptable digest algorithms for signing the authentication data are not discoverable.
  • The key derivation function (KDF) is hardwired to SHA-1.
  • The acceptable digest algorithms for signing client X.509 certificates are not discoverable.

The motivation is stated directly. In August 2004, Xiaoyun Wang's research group reported collisions in MD4, alongside attacks on later hash functions including MD5 and SHA-1. The IETF then called for protocols to support multiple cryptographic algorithms and clean transition strategies, as recommended by BCP 201 (RFC 7696).

The fix has two parts. New KDFs, identified by object identifiers, are negotiated between the client and the Key Distribution Center (KDC). And new structures let the client discover which Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) digest algorithms the KDC supports.
sections.eli5: People found that the old lock could be picked. The fix is a way for both sides to ask what other locks the other one has, and agree on a stronger one.

sections.title: The paChecksum Problem
sections.content:
The paChecksum from RFC 4556 binds the client's pre-authentication data to the Kerberos request body, which also stops the request body from being tampered with. SHA-1 is the only checksum algorithm RFC 4556 allows, so this facility depends on the collision resistance of SHA-1.

When the reply key is delivered by public key encryption, the asChecksum in the KDC reply protects the clear text and the binding between the pre-authentication and the ticket messages. When the reply key is delivered using Diffie-Hellman, SHA-1 in the paChecksum is a weak protection, and nothing else cryptographically binds the Authentication Service (AS) request to the ticket response.

For the Diffie-Hellman case, the new KDF selected by the KDC supplies that binding and integrity protection. The paChecksum itself is not changed and stays at SHA-1.
sections.eli5: The old seal on the letter used a weak glue. Instead of replacing the glue, the new design adds a second seal that is made from the whole conversation.

sections.title: Discovering Digest Algorithms Through Errors
sections.content:
Two existing PKINIT errors gain optional typed data. In both cases the KDC MAY include a list of acceptable digest algorithms in decreasing order of preference. The data is DER-encoded ASN.1.

  • KDC_ERR_DIGEST_IN_SIGNED_DATA_NOT_ACCEPTED can carry a TD_CMS_DATA_DIGEST_ALGORITHMS element (type 111). Its data is a SEQUENCE OF AlgorithmIdentifier naming the CMS digest algorithms the KDC accepts for signing CMS data. This can help troubleshooting when none of the client's algorithms is supported by the KDC.
  • KDC_ERR_DIGEST_IN_CERT_NOT_ACCEPTED can carry a TD_CERT_DIGEST_ALGORITHMS element (type 112). Its allowedAlgorithms field lists the digest algorithms a certification authority may use to sign the client's X.509 certificate and that the KDC accepts. An optional rejectedAlgorithm field names the algorithm that was rejected.
sections.eli5: If the server says no, it can now also say which kinds of handwriting it would have accepted, so you know what to fix.

sections.title: The New Key Derivation Functions
sections.content:
PKINIT turns the Diffie-Hellman shared secret into a Kerberos reply key with a KDF. RFC 8636 defines four new ones under id-pkinit-kdf, named for the hash they use: SHA-1 (1), SHA-256 (2), SHA-512 (3) and SHA-384 (4).

All of them use the one-step key derivation method of NIST SP 800-56A (Section 5.8.2.1, with the ASN.1 format for FixedInfo) and SP 800-56C (Section 4.1, option 1 for the auxiliary function H). The hash is computed over a counter, the shared secret Z and OtherInfo, and the outputs are concatenated and truncated to the key data length. The AS reply key is the result of random-to-key() applied to that keying material.

OtherInfo includes the KDF's own identifier, the client principal name, the ticket-granting server principal name and a PkinitSuppPubInfo structure. That structure contains the enctype of the reply key, the DER encoding of the client's AS-REQ and the DER encoding of the PA-PK-AS-REP in the KDC reply. Including the whole exchange is what cryptographically binds the pre-authentication data to the ticket request and response.
sections.eli5: The shared secret is mixed with a description of the entire conversation before the key is made. If anyone changed the conversation, the two sides would end up with different keys.

sections.title: Negotiating the KDF
sections.content:
The client adds a supportedKDFs field to AuthPack: an unordered set of KDFs it supports, each given as an object identifier in a KDFAlgorithmId. The KDC replies with a new optional kdf field in DHRepInfo naming its choice.

If the request has supportedKDFs, a conforming KDC MUST pick one the client supports and report it in kdf. If none is acceptable, it MUST reply with the new error KDC_ERR_NO_ACCEPTABLE_KDF (100). If the field is absent, the KDC MUST omit kdf and use the KDF from RFC 4556.

If the client sent supportedKDFs but the reply has no kdf, the client can conclude that the KDC is not updated, or that the exchange was subjected to a downgrade attack. Whether to reject such a reply is a matter of local policy; if compatibility with non-updated KDCs is not a concern, the reply should be rejected. Implementations conforming to this specification MUST support id-pkinit-kdf-ah-sha256.
sections.eli5: The client hands over a list of locks it knows. The server picks one and tells the client which. If the server does not name one, the client gets suspicious.

sections.title: Working With Older Software
sections.content:
The design is meant to coexist with unmodified implementations. Because the error data is typed data, an old client simply ignores digest-list elements it does not recognize, and an old KDC just looks like a new KDC that chose not to include a list.

An old client never sends supportedKDFs, so the KDC omits kdf and uses the RFC 4556 KDF, or rejects the request if local policy forbids the old KDF. A new client talking to an old KDC sends supportedKDFs, which the KDC ignores as an unknown extension. The client MUST then use the RFC 4556 KDF or reject the reply if local policy forbids it.
sections.eli5: New and old versions can still talk. The new one asks extra questions, the old one does not notice, and they fall back to the old way unless a rule says that is not allowed.

sections.title: Downgrade Attacks and Their Limits
sections.content:
Negotiation that is not authenticated lets an active attacker perform a downgrade attack, so only secure values should be accepted. The RFC walks through where that can happen:

  • The digest lists in the two error messages are unauthenticated, so an attacker can forge the errors to push a client toward a weaker algorithm. Acceptance is a matter of local policy.
  • The client's supportedKDFs is protected by the signature on signedAuthPack. If that signature algorithm is vulnerable to collision attacks, or the client uses anonymous PKINIT and does not sign, an attacker may remove or alter the list.
  • The kdf field in the KDC reply is unauthenticated, although altering it will likely cause a decryption failure at the client rather than a successful downgrade.
  • The paChecksum remains SHA-1. If a different request body is substituted by attacking SHA-1, the KDC will not notice, but a client using a new KDF will detect it by failing to decrypt the reply.

Which hash functions the KDC uses in its signature, and which the client accepts, is also a matter of local policy.
sections.eli5: A sneaky person could pretend the server only knows weak locks. The design makes this hard, and in most cases the sneaky change just makes the key fail to work.

sections.title: IANA and Test Vectors
sections.content:
IANA assigned two entries in the Kerberos "Pre-authentication and Typed Data" registry: TD-CMS-DIGEST-ALGORITHMS as 111 and TD-CERT-DIGEST-ALGORITHMS as 112.

The RFC also includes test vectors for the KDF, using a common 256-byte all-zero secret value, for SHA-1 with enctype 18, SHA-256 with enctype 18 and SHA-512 with enctype 16, and Appendix A contains the updated PKINIT ASN.1 module.
sections.eli5: The official list of numbers got two new entries, and the document includes practice answers so builders can check their work.

messages.note: Sent instead if none of the client's KDFs is acceptable.

items.label: id-pkinit-kdf-ah-sha1
items.desc: SP800-56A hash-based KDF using SHA-1; 160 output bits.

items.label: id-pkinit-kdf-ah-sha256
items.desc: Using SHA-256; 256 output bits. Implementations MUST support it.
